meta.title: The Same Ladder in Any Key
meta.summary: The five forms in any key are the same C-A-G-E-D wheel entered at a different point, and even F, with no open chord of its own, sits on it exactly where the movable nut predicts.

spans.text: Every diagram, every dot, every fret number in this pathway so far has been C major. That was a teaching choice, not a limit — and this is where it lifts.
Here is the ladder, nut upward, in six keys, with the order the forms occur in as you climb:
Read down the cycle column and it looks like six different orders. It's one order. Every row above is the same loop —
C → A → G → E → D → C
— read from a different starting point. Changing key changes where you enter the wheel. It changes nothing about which way it turns or which form follows which.
Look at the nut-most form in each row above:

. That's not a coincidence. The five forms are the five open major chord shapes, and each one sits at the nut in exactly the key it's named for. Chapter 1 told you the letter names the form, not the chord — this is where the letters came from in the first place.
Same five bands, same order, same overlaps. The only thing that moved is which band starts at the nut — in C it's the C form; in G it's the G form, one step further round the wheel.

. That's not an accident either — it's chapter 1's movable-nut argument, cashed out. F is a semitone above E, so the open E chord moved up one fret spells F. It's also exactly why the F barre is the first barre chord almost everyone learns: in this key there is no open shape to fall back on, so the nut has to be a finger from the very first fret.
The general rule, worth stating once: in any key, the form nearest the nut is the one named after the open chord nearest below that key's root.

One more way to place the ladder, and it's the best sentence in this chapter. Chapter 3 found that in
— are the C major pentatonic, played straight up the low E string. That's true in every key: the five barre frets are always that key's own major pentatonic on the low E string.
The wheel never turns. Only the door you enter it through changes — the key decides where the ladder starts, not what it's made of.
Transposing the ladder isn't a new skill sitting on top of everything else this pathway taught. It's chapter 3's five-note scale, moved.

props.caption: The E form in G major — the same shape you know from C, five frets lower.

spans.text: you already learned. Same seventeen dots, same shape, five frets lower — the first time in this pathway the same form has shown up in a different key.
One caution before you go looking at other keys yourself: near the nut, a window can be cut short by the nut itself. In G, the G form is drawn frets
rather than five wide, because one fret of it would sit behind the nut if the nut weren't there. It's the same form, with less room to draw it in — not a smaller shape.

, set the root to anything other than C, and leave the position toggle on CAGED. Same five windows, same five names, a different key underneath — and now you know why they line up exactly the way they do.
